cim: Radiology, Mathematics, Artificial Intelligence, And Human Understanding
cim_eredeti: Radiology, Mathematics, Artificial Intelligence, And Human Understanding
szoveg_eredeti:
Magic eight ball generating predictions.

Recently, mathematician Steven Strogatz wrote an excellent essay describing the upheaval within the world of mathematics caused by the latest advances in artificial intelligence. His article is well worth reading, but one passage in particular caught my eye. He quoted Curtis McMullen, a math professor at Harvard and a Fields Medalist: "Mathematics is not radiology. It is more like art or philosophy, and in fact, human understanding is what it is all about."

Strogatz elaborated on this point, noting that in arenas like radiology we don't understand exactly how AI arrives at a conclusion, but physicians will act on the results anyways: "If an AI model correctly predicts that you're at heightened risk of developing breast cancer in the next five years, should you care that it can't explain why, and neither can your radiologist? When lives are at stake, understanding becomes less urgent than just knowing the answer."

As a radiologist, I'd like to respond to his question. Just for background, I have been a practicing radiologist for over 30 years. I also have an undergraduate degree in mathematics from MIT (but not a PhD). My father was a PhD mathematics professor for many years before he retired, and I have gotten to know many excellent radiologists and mathematicians over the years.

I completely recognize that for mathematicians, understanding how a result was derived or how a theorem was proved is of paramount importance. This is the heart of contemporary research mathematics.

However, radiologists also strongly desire fundamental understanding of disease processes in service of interpreting medical images. The best radiologists have a keen grasp of anatomy, physiology, and pathophysiology, and they utilize that knowledge every time they interpret a patient's CT or MRI scan.

Radiologists also recognize the limits of biomedical knowledge. By necessity, we employ probabilistic thinking and Bayesian analysis when appropriate in the face of incomplete knowledge. And we will gladly use AI tools that help facilitate patient diagnoses even if we don't fully understand how those tools work.

But it would inaccurate to portray radiologists as uncaring about "understanding." One of our major professional journals is Radiology: Artificial Intelligence. This journal is devoted to "emerging applications of machine learning and artificial intelligence in the field of imaging." A recurrent theme in the journal articles is validating the reliability and limitations of AI tools, understanding how they work, and knowing when those AI tools should (or should not) be trusted for patient care.

As Strogatz has noted, there is an FDA-approved AI tool that can take a patient's mammogram images and make reliable predictions of her breast cancer risk 5 years in the future, well before a cancer actually appears. The tool does not diagnose existing cancers, nor does it guarantee that a patient will develop breast cancer in the future. Instead, the Breast Cancer Research Foundation explains that the tool "estimates the likelihood of developing breast cancer within a specified period of time. This information may help clinicians identify women who could benefit from additional screening, closer monitoring, preventive medications, lifestyle interventions, or other risk-reduction approaches."

Similarly, a new AI system appears to be able to detect prostate cancer on MRI scans as accurately as a good human radiologist. In neither case, do human physicians know exactly how the AIs arrived at their results. All we know is that there is a statistically proven correlation between the AI prediction and the presence of a disease condition.

However, the use of statistically correlated data without full knowledge of the underlying causal mechanism is not new in medicine. This was already the case for many classic medical signs prior to the era of AI. For example, a certain deformity of the fingernails called "clubbing" has a well-known statistical association with some significant heart and lung diseases. This was known to physicians as far back as 2500 years, when described by Hippocrates.

Physicians will act on the clinical indicator of clubbing even we still don't known exactly why this particular fingernail shape is linked to certain lung diseases. If your fingernails develop clubbing, your physician will likely order additional tests to determine if you have an underlying serious problem. Nor have researchers given up on trying to discover the causal link between fingernail clubbing and the underlying diseases. (One plausible theory is that clubbing is caused by elevated levels of a compound known as "vascular endothelial growth factor" which is seen in certain diseases.)

Similarly radiologists might not yet know how an AI diagnoses certain diseases. But like mathematicians, we are always seeking to improve our human understanding of the causal link between the AI result and the underlying biological processes.

To this end, there is active research in the field of "Explainable Artificial Intelligence" (XAI), in which an AI system explains its "reasoning" to human physicians. For example, if an XAI system analyzes a chest x-ray and make a diagnosis of pneumonia, it will also generate a "heat map" showing the suspicious region of the lung along with a description of the abnormality. Many physicians and patients will naturally prefer a medical AI that enhances human understanding over a mysterious "black box" medical AI that spits out diagnoses like a "Magic 8 Ball" toy.

In summary: Radiologists are willing to employ AI tools that have been statistically validated to provide reliable diagnoses, even if we don't yet fully understand how those tools work. But radiologists are not content to stop there. We also continually seek to improve genuine human understanding of how AI works in our field as a matter of professional responsibility for ourselves and for our patients.

This article was originally published on Forbes.com
